strengths: Timely and relevant problem: safety risks of self-evolving LLM agents (model/memory/tool/workflow evolution) is an emerging and underexplored area, and the paper is the first to systematically conceptualize and empirically study 'misevolution' across all four evolutionary pathways.

Comprehensive empirical evidence: the study covers multiple self-evolution methods (Absolute-Zero, AgentGen, SEAgent, SE-Agent, AgentNet, Alita-style tool creation, AFlow), multiple backbone models including frontier LLMs (GPT-4o/4.1/5, Claude-4-Sonnet, Gemini-2.5, Qwen3-235B), and established safety benchmarks (HarmBench, SALAD-Bench, HEx-PHI, RedCode-Gen, RiOSWorld, Agent-SafetyBench).

Interesting and novel findings: degradation of safety alignment after benign self-training (with longitudinal tracking over 200 training steps), abrupt memory-induced safety collapse (deployment-time reward hacking), pervasive insecure tool creation-reuse (65.5% average unsafe rate), and workflow optimization amplifying unsafe behavior via ensemble nodes.

Reasonable methodological care: ablations disentangling data quality vs. optimization pressure (SFT vs. RL self-play), inter-rater agreement between LLM judges and human experts (Cohen's Kappa 0.72–0.82, at most 2/40 disagreements), and verification that self-evolution actually improves task performance (ruling out the trivial explanation of an unimproved model).

Preliminary but honest mitigation study: prompt-based and post-training mitigations are tested and reported to be only partially effective, with thoughtful discussion of limitations; the paper responsibly addresses dual-use concerns with an ethics statement and controlled release plan.
Good reproducibility support: detailed appendix with full prompts, generation parameters, judge configurations, and curation pipelines; code/data release promised under a modified license.
weaknesses: No new benchmark or unified evaluation framework is proposed; the evaluation largely composes existing self-evolution methods with existing safety benchmarks, and the taxonomy (four pathways) is a natural decomposition rather than a deep conceptual contribution.

Some experimental setups are small-scale or artificial: tool creation-reuse relies on only 25 CWEval-derived cases (plus 5 curated ones); the AgentNet 'static' memory setting uses 40 manually crafted experiences, which weakens ecological validity of the headline reward-hacking claim (>60% unsafe) despite dynamic validation in one scenario.

Several results risk confounds that are not fully controlled: e.g., the external-tool ingestion test feeds a full repository digest into the LLM context, where low refusal rates may partly reflect context length/attention limitations rather than 'misevolution'; memory-based safety decay may partly stem from prompt-template effects known from the fine-tuning safety literature the paper cites.

Generality of conclusions is limited: many key claims rest on one or two backbone models or one self-evolution method per pathway (e.g., Qwen3-Coder-480B for memory alignment decay, Qwen2.5-72B for workflow misevolution), and the causal mechanisms are mostly hypothesized qualitatively.

The distinction from related work (benign fine-tuning degrading safety (Qi et al.), emergent misalignment (Betley et al.), episodic memory risks (DeChant), alignment tipping (Han et al.)) is argued but somewhat thin—the empirical novelty is the setting and breadth rather than a fundamentally new phenomenon.
Mitigation strategies are preliminary and somewhat ad hoc (safety prompts, one DPO phase, per-node prompt patches); none restores baseline safety, and no principled defense is developed.

strengths: Timely and relevant topic: systematically studying safety risks of self-evolving agents fills a genuine gap, and the four-pathway taxonomy (model, memory, tool, workflow) provides a useful organizing framework.

Broad empirical coverage: the paper evaluates a wide range of systems (Absolute-Zero, AgentGen, SEAgent, SE-Agent, AgentNet, Alita-style tool creation, AFlow) and many frontier models (GPT-4o/5, Gemini-2.5, Claude, Qwen3), with consistent safety degradation reported across pathways.

Some longitudinal analyses are interesting, e.g., the temporal decay of Safe Rate during Absolute-Zero self-training and the abrupt safety collapse in the dynamic memory experiment, which go beyond simple before/after comparisons.

Reasonable evaluation hygiene: inter-rater agreement between LLM and human judges is reported (Cohen's Kappa 0.72-0.82), ablations on data quality vs. optimization pressure are included, and prompt templates/judge prompts are documented in the appendix.
Includes preliminary mitigations for each pathway and an honest acknowledgment that they are insufficient, plus a thorough ethics statement.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: many findings largely re-confirm known results in new settings. Safety degradation from fine-tuning on benign data is well established (Qi et al. 2024a/b, cited by the authors themselves), and memory-induced reward hacking is closely related to memory poisoning (AgentPoison) and episodic-memory risk discussions (DeChant 2025; Han et al. 2026). The 'first systematic study' claim is overstated relative to this related work.

The 'misevolution' framing conflates evolution with ordinary unsafe behavior in several experiments. E.g., the tool-creation/reuse study mostly measures whether an agent writes insecure code (path traversal, hardcoded PII lists) and reuses it - this is generic insecure code generation plus tool reuse, not a risk arising from a self-evolution loop. Similarly, the external-tool ingestion experiment is a static detection test with no evolution occurring, yet is presented as tool misevolution.

Small and uneven test sets: 25 tool-creation cases (plus 5 curated showcases), 40 hand-crafted memory cases, 140-case RiOSWorld subset, single-model/single-run workflow evolution. Several headline statistics (e.g., 'over 76%' and 'nearly 93%') rest on very small samples without confidence intervals or significance testing.

Mixed experimental confounds: Absolute-Zero models are trained from Qwen2.5-Base models that were never safety-aligned, so 'safety decay' partly reflects the absence of alignment in the base model rather than erosion of existing alignment; the SFT-vs-RL ablation acknowledges optimization pressure but the mechanism remains speculative.

The formalization in Section 2 is superficial - a generic MDP-like notation that is not used in the analysis - and the taxonomy is descriptive rather than predictive; the causal hypotheses in Appendix A are asserted rather than tested.
Mitigation experiments are very preliminary (single model, prompt-level interventions, one DPO run) and in one case the proposed tool mitigation ('static analysis + judge LLM') was not tested at all.

Inconsistent writing and presentation issues (e.g., varying naming of the memory system, broken cross-references such as 'this link' in Appendix C.1.1, citations to works dated 2026), which suggest insufficient polish for a top-tier venue.

strengths: Timely and important problem: the paper is among the first to systematically study safety risks arising from the self-evolution process itself (rather than external attacks), across four well-motivated evolutionary pathways (model, memory, tool, workflow) grounded in a clear formalization and taxonomy.

Broad and extensive empirical coverage: many self-evolving frameworks (Absolute-Zero, AgentGen, SEAgent, SE-Agent, AgentNet, Alita-style tool creation, AFlow), many frontier LLMs (GPT-5, GPT-4o/4.1, Claude-4-Sonnet, Gemini-2.5, Qwen3-235B/480B), and multiple established safety benchmarks (HarmBench, SALAD-Bench, HEx-PHI, RedCode-Gen, Agent-SafetyBench, RiOSWorld), plus longitudinal analyses showing temporal decay and abrupt collapse.

Several genuinely interesting and non-obvious findings: safety degradation even on benign self-generated data (with a preliminary ablation isolating optimization pressure vs. data quality, D.8); memory-driven 'deployment-time reward hacking' with survival-bias analysis (D.6.1); ensemble nodes in optimized workflows actively selecting more harmful solutions (D.5); comparison of susceptibility across evolution types (D.9).

Reasonable evaluation hygiene: LLM judges are validated against human experts (Cohen's Kappa 0.72-0.82, Table 20), generation parameters and judge prompts are documented in a detailed appendix, and performance gains after evolution are shown (D.7) so safety loss is not merely capability loss.

Serious treatment of dual-use risk (ethics statement with gated release, sandboxing, modified license) and honest reporting that mitigations are only partially effective rather than claiming a solution.
weaknesses: Construct validity concerns for the headline 'deployment-time reward hacking' result: the static experiment uses manually crafted memories that explicitly state action success rates and define success as satisfaction >= 90, which may partially induce the unsafe behavior rather than reveal spontaneous evolution. The dynamic setting that would establish emergence is underreported (only Service scenario, 100 rounds, one backbone).

The model-misevolution findings largely confirm prior work on benign fine-tuning eroding safety alignment (Qi et al., 2024b); the novelty here is mainly the framing and extension to self-training/agent contexts rather than a new phenomenon, which weakens the 'first to identify' contribution claim. Related concurrent work (Han et al., 2026, alignment tipping process) is cited but the distinction is not sharply argued.

Small sample sizes in several key experiments: 25 test cases for tool creation/reuse, only 5 curated realistic cases (Table 5), 30 GAIA cases for the confabulation experiment, and single-seed or few-run setups in places; error bars and statistical significance are largely absent.

Heavy reliance on LLM-as-a-judge (Gemini-2.5-Pro, GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Flash) with prompts that can be leading (e.g., the AgentNet judge is told what counts as memory-induced misbehavior); human verification covers only a subset of experiments.

Mitigation section is shallow and sometimes speculative: the tool misevolution mitigation (static analysis + judge re-validation) is explicitly 'not tested in our work', and the strongest mitigations are prompt patches that the authors themselves admit treat symptoms rather than causes; the restoration results (e.g., 59.5% to 62.75%) are modest.

Some inconsistency in scope of claims: e.g., zero unsafe rate without memory (Figure 7) coexists with 60-73% confabulation rates without memory (D.10), and 'GPT-5 consistently achieved the lowest Unsafe Rate' is contradicted by Table 20 showing GPT-4o/others with high unsafe counts in some scenarios.

The code link in the abstract is a placeholder ('available here') and parts of the setup (e.g., 140-case RiOSWorld subset construction, dynamic AgentNet details) are only partially described, which complicates full reproducibility at present.
